questions.q: The number of real roots of the equation ${e}^{4x} + 2{e}^{3x} - {e}^{x} - 6 = 0$ is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given that

${e}^{4x} + 2{e}^{3x} - {e}^{x} - 6 = 0$

Let ${e}^{x} = t$, $t > 0$

$f ( t ) = {t}^{4} + 2{t}^{3} - t - 6$
$f ' ( t ) = 4{t}^{3} + 6{t}^{2} - 1$

${f}^{' '} ( t ) = 12{t}^{2} + 12t > 0$ $( t > 0 )$

$f ' ( t )$ is increasing function

Now ${f}^{'} ( 0 ) = - 1$

${f}^{'} ( 1 ) = 9$

By using Intermediate value theorem there exists a root for $f\left(x\right) = 0$if $f\left(\alpha\right)f\left(\beta\right) < 0 ⇒ f\left(\gamma\right) = 0, \gamma \in \left(\alpha, \beta\right)$

So ${f}^{'} ( \beta ) = 0$

Hence, only one real root.

$f\left(x\right): \left[0,2\right] \to R$ and $f^{''}\left(x\right) > 0$ for $x \in [ 0,2 ]$
~ $⇒ f^{'} ( x )$ is increasing for $x \in [ 0,2 ]$
Now, $ϕ ( x ) = f ( x ) + f ( 2 - x )$
~ ~ $⇒ {ϕ}^{'}\left(x\right) = f^{'}\left(x\right) - f' ( 2 - x )$

$

questions.solution:
Given:

$f\left(x\right) = x^{3} - 6x^{2} + ax + b$

Solving both equations, we get

$a = 8, b = 0$

$∴ f \left(x\right) = x^{3} - 6x^{2} + 8x$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = x\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 4\right)$

Now,

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 3x^{2} - 12x + 8$

Now,

If~$f^{'}\left(x\right) = - 1$

$⇒ 3x^{2} - 12x + 8 = - 1$

$⇒ 3x^{2} - 12x + 9 = 0$

$⇒ x^{2} - 4x + 3 = 0$

$⇒ x^{2} - 3x - x + 3 = 0$

$⇒ \left($x - 1\right)\left($x - 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ x = 1, 3$

Since,~${x}_{1} \in \left($2, 4\right)$, therefore~${x}_{1} = 3$.

And,

$f^{'}\left($x\right) = 0$

$⇒ 3x^{2} - 12x + 8 = 0$

$⇒ x = $\dfrac{12 \pm \sqrt{144 - 96}}{6}

$⇒ x = $\dfrac{12 \pm \sqrt{48}}{6}

$⇒ x = $\dfrac{12 \pm 4\sqrt{3}}{6} = \dfrac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{3}}{3}

$⇒ x = 2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},$2 - $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}

Then,~ \left($2 + \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) \in \left(2, 4\right)$

Hence,~${x}_{2} = 2 + \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}$

So,~${S}_{1}$~is true.

Now,

$f^{'}\left($x\right) = \left(x - \left(2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\right) \left($x - \left($2 - \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\right)$

Sign scheme for~$f^{'} \left(x\right)$~is as follows:

$f^{'} \left($x\right) > 0 ∀ x \in \left(- \infty ,$2 - \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)∪ \left($2 + \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}, \infty\right),$hence it is increasing.

$f^{'} \left(x\right) < 0 ∀ x \in \left($2 - $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3},$2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right),~hence it is decreasing.

So,~${x}_{4} = \left(2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right).

Now,

$2f^{'} \left({x}_{3}\right) = $\sqrt{3}$f \left({x}_{4}\right)

$⇒ 2 \left[3{x}_{3}^{2} - 12{x}_{3} + 8\right] = $\sqrt{3}\left($2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right) \left(2 + \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} -2\$right)\left($2 + $\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} -$4\right)$

$⇒ 2 \left[3{x}_{3}^{2} - 12{x}_{3} + 8\right] = \sqrt{3} \left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} +2\right) \left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} -2\right)$

$⇒ 2 \left[$3{x}_{3}^{2} - 12{x}_{3} + 8\right] = $2\left(\dfrac{12}{9} -$4\right)$

$⇒ \left[$3{x}_{3}^{2} - 12{x}_{3} + 8\right] = - $\dfrac{8}{3}

$⇒ 9{x}_{3}^{2} - 36{x}_{3} + 32 = 0$

$⇒ {x}_{3} = $\dfrac{36 \pm \sqrt{1296 - 1152}}{18} = \dfrac{36 \pm 12}{18}

$⇒ {x}_{3} = $\dfrac{8}{3}, \dfrac{4}{3}

So,~${S}_{2}& is true.

questions.q: The function $f\left(x\right) = 2x + 3x\dfrac{2}{3}, x \in R$, has
options: exactly one point of local minima and no point of local maxima
exactly one point of local maxima and no point of local minima
exactly one point of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
exactly two points of local maxima and exactly one point of local minima
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: $f ( x ) = 2x + 3 ( x) \dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ f^{'} \left($x\right) = 2 + 2x$\dfrac{- 1}{3}

$⇒ f^{'}\left($x\right) = 2\left($1 + $\dfrac{1}{x\dfrac{1}{3}}\right)

$⇒ f^{'} \left(x\right) = 2 \left(\dfrac{x\dfrac{1}{3} + 1}{x\dfrac{1}{3}}\right)

The function changes from positive to negative at $x = 1$ and from negative to positive at $x = 0$

So, the point of local maxima \left(M\right)$ is at $x = - 1$ and the point of local minima \left(m\right)$ at $x = 0$

questions.q: If $f \left(x\right) = x^{2} + g^{'}  \left($1\right)x + g^{"}\left($2\right)$ and~$g  \left($x\right) = f \left($1\right)x^{2} + xf^{'}\left($x\right) + f^{"}\left($x\right)$,~then the value of $f  \left($4\right) - g \left($4\right)$ is equal to _____ .$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given:

$f \left(x\right) = x^{2} + g^{'} \left($1\right)x + g^{"}\left($2\right)$

$⇒ f^{'} \left($x\right) = 2x + g^{'} \left($1\right)$

$⇒ f^{"}\left($x\right) = 2$

Now,

$g \left($x\right) = f \left($1\right)x^{2} + xf^{'}\left($x\right) + f^{"}\left($x\right)$

$⇒ $g\left($x\right) = $f\left($1\right)x^{2} + $x\left[$2x + g^{'}\left($1\right)\right] + 2$

$⇒ $g\left($x\right) = $\lleft[f\left(1\right) + 2\right]x^{2} + g^{'}\left(1\right)x + 2$

$⇒ g^{'} \left(x\right) = 2f \left(1\right)x + 4x + g^{'}\left(1\right) . . . . \left(1\right)$

$⇒ g^{"} \left(x\right) = 2f \left(1\right) + 4 . . . \left(2\right)$

Put~$x = 1$~in~ \left(1\right)$, then we get

$2f\left(1\right) + 4 = 0$

$⇒ f\left(1\right) = - 2$

$∴ g^{"}\left(2\right) = 2f\left(1\right) + 4 = 0$

Now,

$f \left(x\right) = x^{2} + g^{'} \left(1\right)x + g^{"}\left(2\right)$

Put~$x = 1$, then we get

$f \left(1\right) = 1 + g^{'} \left(1\right) + g^{"}\left(2\right)$

$⇒ g^{'}\left(1\right) = - 3$

So,

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 2x - 3$

$f\left(x\right) = x^{2} - 3x + c$

Since,~$f\left(1\right) = - 2 ⇒ c = 0$

So,

$f\left(x\right) = x^{2} - 3x$

And,~

$g \left(x\right) = f \left($1\right)x^{2} + xf^{'}\left($x\right) + f^{"}\left($x\right)$

$⇒ $g\left($x\right) = - 2x^{2} + $x\left($2x - 3\right) + 2$

$⇒ $g\left($x\right) = - 3x + 2$

Hence,~f\left($4\right) - $g\left($4\right) = 4 + 10 = 14$

$

questions.q: The number of distinct real roots of the equation& $x^{5}\left(x^{3} - x^{2} - x + 1\right) + x\left(3x^{3} - 4x^{2} - 2x + 4\right) - 1 = 0$& is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$x^{5}\left(x^{3} - x^{2} - x + 1\right) + x\left(3x^{3} - 4x^{2} - 2x + 4\right) - 1 = 0$

Now on rearranging we get

$⇒ x^{8} - x^{7} - x^{6} + x^{5} + 3x^{4} - 4x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 4x - 1 = 0$

$⇒ x^{7}\left(x - 1\right) - x^{5}\left(x - 1\right) + 3x^{3}\left(x - 1\right) - x\left(x^{2} - 1\right) - 2x\left(x - 1\right) + x - 1 = 0$

$⇒ \left(x - 1\right)\left(x^{7} - x^{5} + 3x^{3} - x\left(x + 1\right) - 2x + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(x - 1\right)\left(x^{5}\left(x^{2} - 1\right) + 3x\left(x^{2} - 1\right) - 1\left(x^{2} - 1\right)\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(x^{2} - 1\right)\left(x - 1\right)\left(x^{5} + 3x - 1\right) = 0$

From above equation it is clearly visible that the root are~$x = \pm 1$~and for~$x^{5} + 3x - 1$

Let~$f\left(x\right) = x^{5} + 3x - 1$,~$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 5x^{4} + 3$

$f^{'}\left(x\right) > 0 ∀ x \in R$, hence it is monotonic in nature so it will have only one root other than~$1 \text{ and } - 1$.

Hence~$3$& real distinct roots.
